Historical biogeography of Middle-East mangroves: paleobotanical evidence
abstract: This paper reconstructs the origin, diversification, and decline of Middle East (ME) mangroves from the Late Creta3ceous to the present using the MESMA database, a comprehensive compilation of fossil pollen and macrofossil records integrated with paleogeographic, tectonic, climatic and sea-level evidence. To date, global paleobiogeographical and evolutionary syntheses of mangroves have emphasized the role of the ME region as either a dispersal corridor or a biogeographical barrier, rather than as a research focus in its own right. The earliest reliable ME mangrove records correspond to Nypa from the Late Cretaceous, when the present-day Arabian Peninsula formed part of the Nubian Plate along the southern Tethyan margin. A potential Nypa precursor was suggested to have occurred in the Albian, but this remains unconfirmed. Mangrove diversification began in the Eocene with the arrival of Avicennia and Acrostichum , followed by Rhizophora in the Oligocene, leading to the highest diversity levels recorded in the region. This diversification is remarkable because it occurred during the Eocene/Oligocene transition, a phase associated with mangrove decline in most other parts of the world. A major biodiversity crisis took place during the Middle Miocene, when regional desertification associated with the Middle Miocene Climatic Transition, likely linked to the Arabia–Eurasia collision and the resulting closure of the Tethys Sea, caused the disappearance of most mangrove elements, leaving only Avicennia and Rhizophora as surviving mangrove-forming taxa. This event established the low-diversity pattern that characterizes present-day ME mangroves. Quaternary records are scarce, but Holocene sequences from southern Arabia document a pronounced reduction of Rhizophora between approximately 6.5 and 4.5 ka BP, coinciding with the termination of the Holocene Humid Period, after which the genus survived only in a few relict areas, whereas the more stress-tolerant Avicennia persisted and became dominant. In contrast to previous studies, this synthesis identifies the ME as a significant region for mangrove evolution per se, rather than merely in relation to other biogeographical regions. The study also highlights substantial gaps in the fossil record and several unresolved questions that provide promising avenues for future research.

title: Cambrian–Devonian reconstructions of East Asian blocks via detrital zircon big data and mixing models
abstract: The tectonic evolution of the Tethyan oceans and the subsequent accretion of East Asian blocks to Eurasia are central to deciphering the geodynamic assembly of the Asian continent. However, the precise paleogeographic configuration of these continental fragments along the northeastern Gondwanan margin remains a subject of intense debate, obscuring our understanding of the episodic lifecycles of the Proto-, Paleo-, and Neo-Tethys oceans and the sequence of Gondwanan fragmentation. Here, we present a robust quantitative paleogeographic reconstruction underpinned by a comprehensive large detrital zircon U-Pb geochronological dataset from key Cambrian to Devonian sedimentary successions of northeastern Gondwana. By employing inverse Monte Carlo mixture modeling to quantitatively partition sediment provenance and terrane affinities, integrated with existing paleomagnetic constraints, we demonstrate that these blocks were arranged in a concentric belt framework along the Gondwanan margin. Our modeling results delineate a structured spatial arrangement. The innermost blocks (Qiangtang, Baoshan, and Sibumasu) were situated proximal to the Indian margin, while the Lhasa terrane is interpreted to be situated adjacent to Australia. An intermediate belt, comprising Indochina and South China, bridged these sectors. The outboard Tarim and North China cratons, following their Cambrian isolation, were incorporated into the margin by the Ordovician, synchronous with the terminal closure of the Proto-Tethys Ocean. This spatial arrangement archives a spatio-temporally diachronous rift-drift narrative. Northward dispersal initiated with these outboard cratons during the Ordovician–Silurian, progressed to the intermediate blocks during the Devonian opening of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean, and culminated in the late Paleozoic rifting of the innermost blocks during the opening of the Neo-Tethys Ocean. We interpret this orderly, inboard-younging unzipping sequence as a first-order geodynamic response to sequential opening of the Tethyan oceans, likely driven by sustained subduction zone rollback. This model provides a unifying framework that reconciles disparate geological datasets and elucidates the staged northward transfer of continental fragments from Gondwana to Asia.

title: Reconstructing phreatic palaeogroundwater levels: A methodological review
abstract: Nature-based water management requires a clear understanding of baseline hydrological regimes. Reconstruction of Palaeogroundwater Level (PGWL) is emerging as an approach to determine past groundwater level as a mean to estimate ‘baseline’ or ‘pre-management’ conditions, thereby providing essential benchmarks to guide such interventions. However, methods for PGWL reconstruction remain fragmented across disciplines. This review synthesizes existing approaches of PGWL reconstruction across multiple disciplines, with a specific focus on phreatic groundwater systems, where water-table depth can be inferred from near-surface environmental archives and related proxies. Such aquifers are among the most vulnerable to depletion under global change. We present a range of reconstruction approaches grouped into three major categories: 1) Historical records provide direct evidence of hydrological condition from documented and measured sources; 2) Proxy methods rely on a combination of natural and anthropogenic geo-archives, including biological indicators, soils, sediment profiles, archaeological features, and geomorphological landforms; and 3) Model-based estimations use mathematical relationships to hindcast PGWLs. For each approach, we synthesize its theoretical foundations, evaluate its practical applicability and limitations, analyse its respective spatiotemporal scales, and illustrate its implementation with representative examples. By unifying scattered knowledge, we establish a critical guide for selecting appropriate reconstruction approaches tailored to specific contexts and objectives. We further propose an integration framework in which historical archives are used as evaluation and calibration datasets to strengthen proxy- and model-based reconstructions. This synthesis ultimately supports more resilient and nature-based water management strategies by providing robust methods for determining baseline conditions in unconfined groundwater systems.

Superposition, stratigraphic disorder, and diagenetic bedding: What Steno, Walter, and Smith did not know about some carbonate successions
abstract: Traditional stratigraphic principles, such as Steno's “Law of Superposition”, Smith's “Principles of Stratigraphy” on lateral continuity, and Walther's “Facies Rule”, assume a straightforward relationship between deposition, time, and lithology. However, in successions containing carbonates, diagenetic processes often disrupt this framework by introducing secondary features that mimic, overprint, or obscure original sedimentary features. Diagenetic bedding, or diabedding, describes the partition of a sedimentary succession into separate units not by depositional processes but by varying degrees of cementation during diagenesis. Various theories exist to describe different mechanisms that lead to the creation of diabedding and the alteration of geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeontological properties. While existing theories agree that these transformations complicate interpretations of litho-, bio-, and cyclostratigraphy, potentially distorting age-depth relationships and facies correlations, there is no consensus between marine burial diagenetic models. These models suggest different underlying mechanisms and, crucially, different impacts on (1) the preservation of key stratigraphic information, (2) the formation of lithifying cements, and (3) CaCO 3 dissolution and redistribution in general. Another problem is that most diagenetic models focus on one particular aspect or endmember, threatening their unifying application. Here, we synthesise key models and empirical observations to highlight the stratigraphic implications of diagenetic overprinting, calling for interdisciplinary approaches and for better awareness and discussion of models between diagenetic schools. Recognising and accounting for diagenetic alteration is essential for accurately interpreting the carbonate rock record and with the ongoing discrepancy between diagenetic models (processes and impacts) an increased effort is necessary to identify transformations in modern deposits to understand the past.

An integrated bio- and chemostratigraphic framework for the Triassic–Jurassic boundary interval and its potential for global correlations
abstract: The Triassic/Jurassic boundary (TJB) interval records one of the major Phanerozoic mass extinctions, commonly linked to the effects of volcanism of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province. However, uncertainties persist regarding the age, duration and synchroneity of events across the boundary, largely because of ambiguities in stratigraphic correlations, even among reference TJB sections. Stratigraphic correlations across the TJB have traditionally been based on the δ 13 C record of the sedimentary organic carbon (δ 13 C org ), while the carbonate carbon-isotope record (δ 13 C carb ) has been long considered unreliable. Here, we reassess inorganic carbon-isotope stratigraphy across the TJB using well-preserved skeletal and bulk carbonate δ 13 C records from reference sections of the Northern Calcareous Alps (Austria) and the Laurasian Seaway (UK). These records are used to build a new δ 13 C carb framework that is anchored to ammonite biostratigraphy and complemented with the sequence of negative δ 13 C org excursions adopted in previous studies. We document reproducible δ 13 C carb patterns consisting of: (1) a prominent negative excursion, corresponding to the initial carbon-isotope excursion of the δ 13 C org record in the topmost Marshi Chronozone and characterised by the minimum point “a”, (2) a positive excursion encompassing the TJB herein named “Triassic/Jurassic Boundary Event” and culminating in the positive peak “b” in the top Tilmanni Chronozone, (3) a negative trend to pre-excursion values with the minimum point “c” documented in the Angulata Chronozone and (4) a second positive excursion encompassing the Hettangian/Sinemurian Boundary and culminating in the positive peak “d” in the Semicostatum Chronozone. These δ 13 C carb patterns appear globally reproducible across deep-sea to shallow-water sections and are potentially extended to the δ 13 C carb signature of pedogenic carbonates in continental records, offering a powerful new tool for global basin-to-land correlations and for understanding carbon-cycle perturbations associated with CAMP volcanism.

Natural gravel beaches and dynamic gravel structures: A systematic review of classifications, cross-shore processes, transferability and knowledge gaps
abstract: Natural gravel beaches provide effective coastal protection through shoreline stabilization, wave energy dissipation, and reduced runup, due to high permeability and dynamic behavior. With increasing climate change pressures and growing interest in nature-based solutions, gravel nourishment –defined here as dynamic gravel structures– is being more widely implemented. However, a comprehensive understanding of the processes governing these systems remains limited. This work therefore explores how sediment composition controls hydro-morpho-sedimentary processes across different gravel beach types, and how this understanding can inform the design of artificial dynamic gravel structures. Permeability is identified as a dominant control in pure gravel beaches, although its effects are strongly coupled with grain size and sediment density, which together govern infiltration capacity and beach stability. In mixed and composite systems, the presence of sand reduces permeability and modifies sediment transport, wave breaking, and swash dynamics. These systems can exhibit seasonal variability, with sand- or gravel-dominated profiles that influence the prevailing processes, driven by variations in wave energy and sediment exchange, which in turn alter permeability, infiltration, and sediment mobility. A dynamic, closed-loop interaction between sediment characteristics, wave forcing, swash, and groundwater processes is identified as the basis for process-based understanding across gravel beach types. Studies of dynamic gravel structures demonstrate their effectiveness for coastal protection, but also highlight limitations linked to incomplete representation of these processes. A classification of structures is proposed, including artificial gravel beaches, gravel nourishment, and dynamic cobble berm revetments, providing a foundation for the development of design guidelines. Key knowledge gaps remain in sand–gravel interactions and process-based modelling, where system complexity limits the development of robust predictive tools.
